title: A House, a Room, and the Stem That Bends

lessons.title: घर (ghar) — house, home
lessons.gloss: house, home — the noun the whole place column is about to be built on, and a cousin of a verb you already own

segments.text: You can point at a place — इथे, तिथे — and you cannot yet NAME one.

segments.instruction: say ithe, then tithe, then ask kuṭhe?

segments.text: घर — ghar — house, home.
माझं घर इथे आहे. — mājhaṁ ghar ithe āhe. — my house is here.
Two letters you have had since chapter six, and a word Marathi uses for both house and home — the building and the belonging, with no second word for the difference.

It comes from Sanskrit गृह (gṛha), and गृह is built on the root ग्रह् (grah-), "to grasp, to hold." You already own that root: it is the one under घेणे, to take. A house, in Marathi's oldest layer, is the thing that holds you.
घर (ghar) is neuter, like कुटुंब. That will matter the moment you put an adjective on it, and it matters now for माझं rather than माझा.

segments.instruction: say की and report that your house is here — mī mhaṇto kī …
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: say **की** and report that your house is here — *mī mhaṇto kī …*]

segments.prompt: Say that your house is here, then that it is there.
acceptedResponses: mājhaṁ ghar ithe āhe; mājhaṁ ghar tithe āhe
माझं घर इथे आहे माझं घर तिथे आहे

feedback.correct: A named place, pointed at two ways.
feedback.incorrect: Swap only ithe for tithe and leave āhe last.

segments.text: Which taught verb shares a root with घर (ghar)? (घेणे — both from grah-, "to hold".) What gender is घर (ghar)? (Neuter.)
Sources: Wiktionary: घर (ghar).

lessons.title: खोली (khoolī) — room
lessons.gloss: room — the inside of the house, and the first thing a Marathi sign or a rental notice names

segments.text: A house has an inside. That inside needs a name before anything can be said to be in it.
खोली — khoolī — room.
माझ्या घरात एक खोली आहे. — mājhyā gharāt ek khoolī āhe. — there is one room in my house.

खोली (khoolī) is feminine, which its -ी ending announces before you are told. It is the word a rental notice uses, the word a hotel uses, and the word you would use for the room you sleep in — Marathi does not have a separate everyday noun for bedroom the way English does; it says the room you do the sleeping in.

The word is the noun of खोल (khool), "deep." A room is a depth cut into a house. Once you know that pair you also know a second, unrelated-looking word: खोली (khoolī) on its own can mean depth, which is the same noun doing its literal job.
That sentence above did something new to घर, and you should notice it now rather than be surprised by it: घर became घरा- (gharā-) before -त. The next lesson is about nothing else.

segments.instruction: say -ण्यासाठी and give a purpose for a room — jhopaṇyāsāṭhī
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: say **-ण्यासाठी** and give a purpose for a room — *jhopaṇyāsāṭhī*]

segments.prompt: Say: my house, and one room.

feedback.incorrect: ghar is neuter and takes mājhaṁ; khoolī is feminine.

segments.text: What gender is खोली (khoolī), and what tells you? (Feminine; the -ी.) What adjective is it built on? (खोल, deep.)
Sources: Wiktionary: खोली (khoolī).

lessons.title: घरा- (gharā-) — the stem a noun takes before a postposition
lessons.gloss: the oblique stem — the one shape change that stands between every noun in this book and every postposition in the next three chapters

segments.text: घर (ghar) became घरात last lesson, and पुणे became पुण्यात back in chapter twelve. Neither one just took an ending. Both changed shape first.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the noun bends before anything is glued to it

segments.text: Marathi puts almost every place, time and direction relation on a postposition — a piece glued to the END of the noun. Chapter twelve showed you one. What it did not say is that the noun does not stay as it is: it first takes an oblique stem, and only then accepts the glue.
घर becomes घरा- (gharā-) becomes घरात पुणे becomes पुण्या- becomes पुण्यात खोली (khoolī) becomes खोली (khoolī)- becomes खोलीत.

Three classes, three answers, and the pattern is worth holding as a shape rather than a list. A neuter noun ending in a consonant takes -आ. A noun ending in -ए takes -या. A feminine noun in -ी does not change at all.

This is the single most load-bearing rule in the book so far, because nothing in the next three chapters works without it. Every one of the five postpositions they teach — madhye, var, khālī, javaḷ and samor — demands the oblique before it, and a Marathi sentence that skips it is not merely clumsy: it is wrong.

segments.instruction: ghar, then gharāt — and hear the extra ā
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ghar*, then *gharāt* — and hear the extra *ā*]

segments.instruction: khoolī, then khoolīt — and hear that nothing was added
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *khoolī*, then *khoolīt* — and hear that nothing was added]

segments.instruction: mī gharāt rāhto — I live in the house
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *mī gharāt rāhto* — I live in the house]

segments.prompt: Put ghar and khoolī into the -t locative and say which one changed shape.

feedback.incorrect: Add -ā to ghar first, then -t. khoolī takes -t straight.

segments.text: What happens to a Marathi noun before a postposition? (It takes an oblique stem first.) Which of the three classes changes least? (Feminine -ी — not at all.)

lessons.title: Ask where, and answer with a place you can name
lessons.gloss: two nouns, one ending, and the bend that only one of them needs

segments.text: Until this chapter, कुठे? could only be answered by pointing. Now it can be answered with a room.

segments.instruction: ithe — and notice you can now answer that question two ways
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ithe* — and notice you can now answer that question two ways]

segments.instruction: say a jevhā … tevhā … sentence about being at home
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: say a *jevhā … tevhā …* sentence about being at home]

segments.instruction: say the line of your message that means I understand Marathi
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: say the line of your message that means *I understand Marathi*]

segments.prompt: Ask where somebody is and answer twice: in the house, then in the room.

feedback.correct: A where-question answered with a named place.
feedback.incorrect: gharāt takes the -ā first; khoolīt does not.

segments.text: Which of घर and खोली (khoolī) changes shape before -त? (घर, to घरा- (gharā-).) Why does that rule matter more than it looks? (Every postposition in the next three chapters needs it.)
